title: Onboarding That Makes the Work and the Culture Understandable
before: A conversation about making a new colleague’s work, review routes, and team norms visible from the first day.

turns.text: This course is Onboarding That Makes the Work and the Culture Understandable. It’s for anyone who helps welcome a new colleague, and especially for supervisors who design onboarding. The idea is that a welcome works best when nothing important is left unsaid, including the unwritten norms that experienced staff follow without thinking about them.

The opening case is familiar. A new analyst understands the policy issue but can’t identify who reviews the first draft, because the guide just says they’ll pick it up. Before reading the delay as poor judgment, the course asks us what local information was actually available. Most of us can remember needing that kind of answer ourselves.

And the course frames onboarding as an entry into meaningful work. It connects people with purpose, expectations, relationships, resources, and support. A completed checklist or a friendly greeting helps, but neither shows that the work is understandable. The practical test is what the arrangement actually makes possible for someone on their first tasks.

The first practice situation shifts to services. A person knows the question they want answered but not the service’s normal sequence. You’ll decide which response is most useful. I like that the course pairs the workplace and the service setting, because unfamiliarity with a system looks very similar in both, and it’s easy to misread in both.

A good welcome also has a sequence. What does someone need before beginning, what helps with the first task, and what becomes useful later? Delivering every resource in one packet doesn’t do that. Access has to be ready too, including equipment, systems, materials, and meeting arrangements. A preventable gap there isn’t proof that the colleague is unprepared.

One distinction I found especially useful is between habit and authority. A team habit isn’t automatically a required process, so it helps to ask where an expectation comes from and what it accomplishes. Genuine requirements should be explained accurately, and unwritten preferences shouldn’t be presented as agency authority just because experienced staff follow them.

The second practice situation builds on that. A new analyst misses a review step that’s only known through informal conversation. You’ll consider what should be examined before anyone makes a broad performance judgment. The course is clear that a newcomer can need orientation and still be accountable for applying the guidance they do receive.

Relationships matter as well. An introduction should explain how a person or role helps with the work, not just list names. A buddy can help locate routine information when the purpose is clear. And belonging shouldn’t become a performance. People don’t need to socialize the same way to contribute and cooperate professionally.

The third situation is about identity. A newcomer is asked to teach a community overview because of their identity, but their stated interest is legislative research. You’ll choose the better approach. The course’s point is that learning about the people we serve belongs in shared professional development, not on whoever the team assumes knows a community.

Near the end, you’ll privately rewrite an instruction that says, you will learn who needs to see the draft as you go. Using a practice review route, you’ll explain the relevant role, the expected result, and where to get clarification, and you’ll mark any real process detail that would need confirming rather than inventing it.

As you work through it, think about your own start on this team, or the last time someone new joined. What did they have to guess? Bring that situation with you. A useful introduction respects the colleague and makes room for real contribution, and it applies again at every transition, whether that’s a new assignment, supervisor, or system.

guidance.title: Where an expectation comes from
guidance.text: When you explain how your team works, try naming the source of each expectation. Is it a policy requirement, a supervisor’s direction, or a habit that grew over time? Habits can be useful, and newcomers still need to know them. Saying which is which helps a new colleague prioritize, ask better questions, and suggest an improvement without seeming to challenge a rule.

guidance.title: The next unfamiliar start
guidance.text: Onboarding doesn’t happen only once. Think about someone on your team who recently changed assignments, systems, or supervisors. Which information or support carried over, and which may have been lost? Is there an unwritten step they would have to discover on their own? What is one thing you could make visible for the next person who starts something new?
